Every day, millions of web pages are updated, replaced, or permanently removed. Valuable information can disappear without warning, leaving gaps in digital history. Archive, more formally known as the Internet Archive, was created to prevent this loss by preserving digital content and making it freely accessible to everyone. What Is Archive? Archive (Internet Archive) is a non-profit organization dedicated to collecting, archiving, and providing free access to digital content. Established in 1996, it functions as a digital memory of the internet, ensuring that online information remains available even after it disappears from the live web. Unlike commercial platforms, Archive operates with an open-access philosophy. Its content includes: Archived web pages Millions of digital books and texts Music and audio recordings Movies and educational videos Software, games, and emulated systems Images, news broadcasts, and historical media Most resources on Archive can be accessed without payment, subscriptions, or mandatory registration. The Mission and Vision of Archive Universal Access to Knowledge Archive’s guiding principle is universal access to all knowledge. The platform aims to remove barriers that prevent people from learning, researching, or preserving cultural heritage. Its vision is based on three key goals: Preservation – Saving digital content before it disappears Accessibility – Making information freely available worldwide Longevity – Ensuring future generations can access historical data By combining technology with a library-centered mission, Archive fills a critical role that no commercial service can fully replace. It allows users to view historical versions of websites by selecting a specific date in time. tool.title: Observer effect (physics)
tool.excerpt: In physics, the observer effect is the disturbance of a system by the act of observation. This is often the result of utilising instruments that, by necessity, alter the state of what they measure in some manner. A common example is checking the pressure in an automobile tire, which causes some of the air to escape, thereby changing the amount of pressure one observes. Similarly, seeing non-luminous objects requires light hitting the object to cause it to reflect that light. While the effects of observation are often negligible, the object still experiences a change. This effect can be found in many domains of physics, but can usually be reduced to insignificance by using various instruments or observation techniques.
